label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said I should put it in writing, so here we are. A proper letter, delivered to your house in Croydon at my own expense. Please appreciate the stamp. Some friendships have become too comfortable with free WhatsApp.

At my birthday, somewhere in the middle of your latest report on the suffering of quantity surveyors, I said you should come and teach maths. You laughed and said if I was serious, I should write you a letter. I suspect you thought that would be the end of it.

Unfortunately for you, I am a teacher. Setting a task and assuming nobody will follow up was a tactical error.

I am serious. I think you would be a good maths teacher, and I want you to come with me to the training partnership’s open evening in Lewisham on **Thursday 19 November, at 6pm**. That is the whole request. Come and find out what it involves. You do not have to resign, sign anything or announce a new chapter on LinkedIn. In fact, please don’t do that last one regardless.

You have been at that firm for nine years. I know being bored with your job does not automatically mean you should do mine. There are plenty of ways to change your life that do not involve persuading a fourteen-year-old to bring a pen to a place they attend every weekday. But when you say every day is the same spreadsheet, and then say it again six months later, I do wonder how many more years you want to give that spreadsheet.

I have known you since Unilag. Long before anyone paid you to check costings, you were tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. Yes, you got an A in further maths. Well done; we have all had sufficient time to recover from the news. But being good at maths is only part of why I am writing.

You could explain it.

There were people who arrived at those sessions already convinced they were stupid. You would sit with them, make one joke, find out where they had got lost and start from there. You didn’t act as if understanding something quickly made you a superior human being. If the first explanation didn’t work, you tried another one. That is a much rarer quality than you think.

And before you tell me that was years ago, let us discuss Christmas. My nephew still talks about you teaching him fractions with portions of jollof rice on plates. You were supposed to be enjoying your Christmas, but somehow you ended up arranging somebody’s lunch into a maths lesson. He remembers it because you made it make sense without making him feel foolish for not understanding it before.

That is the part I keep coming back to. You are patient. You are funny. You can explain things without making people feel small. I think children would really take to you. Some would still test your patience beyond anything you currently believe possible, but we will come to those shareholders shortly.

Last month, Damola, one of my Year 11 boys, finally understood simultaneous equations. We had been at it for three weeks. Three weeks of trying, getting stuck, going back, trying again. Then something clicked and he shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped.

I wish you could have seen his face. He was delighted and slightly annoyed, as though I had personally been hiding the simplicity of the thing from him.

I went home happy that day. There was still marking in my bag. Nothing else about the job had magically sorted itself out. But a boy who had spent weeks thinking he couldn’t do something now knew he could. I had helped him get there.

You said on your last birthday, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” I remember because you were being serious, and I didn’t want to spoil it by pointing out how dramatic you sounded.

I am not saying your work now doesn’t matter. Buildings need people who know what they are doing with the money, and I would prefer mine to have been properly costed. But I do think there are parts of you that your job barely gets to use. The patience, the humour, the pleasure you take in helping somebody understand. It seems a shame for all of that to appear only at Christmas, between servings of rice.

Now for the part that would mysteriously disappear if this were a recruitment brochure.

Teaching is hard. The marking can feel endless. Behaviour on some days is proper wahala. You can prepare a lesson carefully and then spend far too much of it dealing with something you could not possibly have planned for. You will repeat instructions you were quite certain you had already given in clear English. You will sometimes go home tired and wonder whether you handled a situation well.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. I am putting that in a letter you can keep, so please recognise the trust involved.

It got better. I learned, asked for help and stopped expecting myself to know how to handle everything immediately. That did not make the job easy, but it made it more manageable. I wouldn’t sell you the good days and then leave you to discover the rest on a wet Tuesday in October. You would rightly abuse me.

There is also the money. The salaried route means you get paid while you train, but you would still be taking a pay drop in that first year. We should not wave that away because the work is meaningful. Meaningful work must still coexist with bills in Croydon.

The route I have in mind lasts one year and starts in September 2027. Applications open soon. At the open evening, you can ask about the actual salary, what the training week looks like, what support you get and how pay progresses afterwards. Get the figures and do your sums. For once, a spreadsheet might help you escape a spreadsheet.

The holidays and pension are worth considering too, though I will not pretend every school holiday is untouched leisure. There is work that follows you home. Still, those things belong in the calculation alongside the pay cut, not as an excuse to ignore it.

And abeg, don’t tell me you are too old. You are 34. A woman in my department started at 41. You would be coming in with years of working experience and maths you have actually used outside an exam paper. You would have plenty to learn about teaching, obviously, but you would not be arriving empty-handed.

At our school in Peckham, we have about 1,100 children. Two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I mention that because the need is real and very close to me. Those children need good, consistent teaching. But our staffing situation is not your personal responsibility, and you should not change careers out of guilt. I want you to consider this because I think you might be good at it, and because it might give you something you have been missing.

So come on the 19th. Thursday, 6pm, Lewisham. I will go with you.

Bring all your difficult questions. Ask about money, workload, behaviour, support and what happens when a trainee struggles. Don’t let anybody answer you entirely in cheerful slogans. Afterwards, we can get something to eat and you can tell me honestly what you think.

If it is not for you, fair enough. I will accept that, and you will still have this letter as evidence that I once bought a stamp.

But give it one evening before you rule it out. You asked whether I was serious. Serious enough to put this through the post, my guy.

Much love,

Your friend from Moremi
